title: Integrated Guide: GPU Fleet, Capacity, Cloud Accounts, Networking, Terraform/IaC Modules, and CI/CD
author: Avery Chen
content:
Overview

This page consolidates our infrastructure engineering guidance for the GPU fleet and capacity planning, cloud account and networking structure, Terraform/IaC module usage, and CI/CD/build pipelines. It combines architecture, SLOs/thresholds, Terraform examples, CI gating patterns, and operational runbooks to provide a single reference for day-1 and day-2 activities.

Scope
- GPU fleet lifecycle: provisioning, autoscaling, upgrades, and decommissioning.
- Capacity targets and headroom policy for production and staging clusters.
- Cloud account topology and VPC networking required for private deployments and hosted services.
- Terraform modules and IaC patterns used by infra teams.
- CI/CD pipeline patterns: plan/apply gating, approvals, canary applies.
- Runbooks for capacity shortage, node failures, and emergency scale-up.

Owners and Contacts
- Primary owner: infra-capacity team (team email: infra-capacity@redwood.example.com).
- Oncall rotation: infra-oncall (PagerDuty).
- Terraform module owner: terraform-modules team (Slack: #infra-iac).
- CI/CD pipeline owner: infra-ci team.

High-level architecture
- Services and components:
  - gpu-manager: service that orchestrates node lifecycle and labels nodes by type (a100-80gb, h100-80gb, t4).
  - fleet-autoscaler: custom controller (k8s) that watches queued workload and issues node pool scale actions via cloud provider APIs.
  - terraform-modules/gpu: reusable modules for node pools, autoscaler policies, and IAM.
  - ci-pipelines/infrastructure: GitHub Actions workflows and Terraform Cloud (or self-hosted Atlantis) integration.
  - metrics & alerting: Datadog + Prometheus exporters + Grafana dashboards (dash IDs in appendix).

Capacity Targets and SLOs (Goals)
- Cluster utilization target: 60% median GPU utilization across production pools during business hours.
- Utilization hard cap: 85% sustained; if sustained > 85% for 10m, trigger scaling policy and page oncall.
- Headroom reserve: maintain 15% spare capacity for burst traffic and failover.
- Pod scheduling latency (due to capacity): P95 < 120s for production queues.
- Node provisioning time (cold create): median 300s, P95 < 600s.
- Preemptible/spot eviction tolerance: workload must gracefully checkpoint within 30s of preemption notice.

Autoscaling and Policies
- Autoscaler modes:
  1. Reactive: scale when queued GPU requests (inference proxy) exceed threshold for 30s.
  2. Predictive: time-of-day scaling using scheduled policies for known traffic patterns (weekday M-F 9:00-18:00 local region).
  3. Buffer pools: small reserved pools per-region and per-customer tier for predictable low-latency requests.

- Terraform-controlled parameters (examples):
  - desired_capacity_min = 2
  - desired_capacity_max = 200
  - scale_up_step = 4
  - scale_down_cooldown = 600 (seconds)

Terraform / IaC Module Guidelines
- Modules live in git: git@github.com:redwood/terraform-modules.git under modules/gpu-node-pool and modules/autoscaler-policy.
- Module contracts (must be stable):
  - inputs: region, instance_type, gpu_type, min_size, max_size, taints, labels, iam_role_arn.
  - outputs: node_pool_id, autoscaler_policy_id, instance_profile.

Example module usage (HCL snippet):

  module "gpu_pool_a100" {
    source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/terraform-modules.git//modules/gpu-node-pool?ref=v1.6.0"
    region = "us-west-2"
    instance_type = "nvidia-a100-80gb"
    gpu_type = "a100"
    min_size = 4
    max_size = 100
    labels = { role = "inference", tier = "prod" }
    taints = ["gpu=true:NoSchedule"]
  }

Module release process:
1. Create feature branch in terraform-modules repo.
2. Add unit tests / terratest.
3. Open PR and request terraform-modules maintainers review.
4. CI must pass linting, fmt, and terratest.
5. Tag semantic version (vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) and publish.

CI/CD and Build Patterns
- Git branching: environment-specific stacks are represented as workspaces (prod, staging, dev). Changes must be proposed via PR against the stack folder.
- Plan policies: all terraform plan outputs are stored in PR checks.
- Apply gating: requires at least two approvers for prod applies (one infra owner + one owner from consuming team).
- Canary applies: for changes that affect node pools or autoscaling, first apply to staging then to a single prod-az as a canary.

Example GitHub Actions workflow (simplified YAML snippet):

  name: terraform-ci
  on: [pull_request]
  jobs:
    terraform-plan:
      runs-on: ubuntu-latest
      steps:
        - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        - name: Setup Terraform
          uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v2
        - name: terraform init
          run: terraform init -backend-config="workspace=${{ matrix.workspace }}"
        - name: terraform fmt & validate
          run: terraform fmt -check && terraform validate
        - name: terraform plan
          run: terraform plan -var-file="${{ matrix.vars_file }}" -out=plan.tfplan
        - name: upload plan
          uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
          with:
            name: terraform-plan
            path: plan.tfplan

Pipeline enforcement:
- No direct pushes to production workspace.
- All applies to prod require gated promotion or manual apply with two approvers.
- Atlantis is allowed for developer-driven applies in non-prod only.

Networking and Cloud Account Topology
- Account layout:
  - management (root) account: central org-level IAM, billing, shared services.
  - prod account(s): region-specific production workloads.
  - staging account(s): mirrors prod for validation.
  - dev account(s): sandbox for teams.

- VPCs and routing:
  - Each account/region pair has a dedicated VPC for the GPU cluster: vpc-<env>-<region>.
  - Subnet naming: private-subnet-<az>-gpu, public-subnet-<az>-bastion.
  - Transit architecture: Transit Gateway for cross-account traffic between control-plane services and S3 endpoints.
  - NAT and egress: use managed NAT gateway pools; prefer VPC endpoints for S3 and ECR.

- Network security:
  - Security groups: allow only necessary ports from control-plane CIDRs.
  - Private endpoints for metrics (Datadog/Prometheus push) and artifact registries.

Runbook: GPU Capacity Shortage (P95 Pod Pending > 120s)
1. Triage (first 5 min)
   - Check dashboards: GPU utilization, pending pods, queue depth. Dashboards: GPU Fleet Overview (dash ID: dash-gpu-001).
   - Query metrics (example Datadog CLI):
     - datadog query "avg:gpu.utilization{cluster:prod}by{nodepool}" --from "now-30m"
   - Check node pool sizes and pending scale actions:
     - kubectl get nodes -l nodepool=prod-a100 -o wide
     - aws autoscaling describe-auto-scaling-groups --names prod-a100-pool

2. Immediate mitigations (5-20 min)
   - If autoscaler is lagging, trigger manual scale up (Terraform or cloud CLI):
     - aws autoscaling set-desired-capacity --auto-scaling-group-name prod-a100-pool --desired-capacity 48
   - If provisioning delay too long, failover to spot/secondary instance types (example):
     - Edit fleet-autoscaler policy to allow h100-80gb preemptible pools as temporary pool.
   - Increase buffer pool size by +10% for the affected region via Terraform change to worker buffer pool. Apply with canary to single AZ first.

3. Post-incident actions (after stabilization)
   - Root cause analysis: collect metrics, autoscaler logs, cloud API throttling errors.
   - Adjust autoscaler thresholds or increase baseline capacity if this is recurring.
   - Update runbook with discovered timings and owners.

4. Escalation
   - If manual scale does not reduce queue within 20 minutes, page infra oncall with incident priority P1. Include attached dashboards and exact commands run.

Node upgrade and maintenance playbook
- Preparation:
  - Validate driver/kernel compatibility matrix (appendix table).
  - Drain nodes in small batches: max 10% of pool at once.
  - Use disruption budget to maintain service availability.
- Upgrade steps:
  1. Create new node pool with target image and drivers.
  2. Shift traffic by updating node selectors on daemonsets and jobs, then cordon and drain old nodes.
  3. Decommission old pool after traffic has fully migrated and monitoring shows normal metrics for 30m.

Kernel / driver compatibility (example)
- NVIDIA driver 535.x -> CUDA 12.1 supported images: redwood-gpu-runtime:cuda12.1-ubuntu22.04
- NVIDIA driver 530.x -> CUDA 11.8 supported images: redwood-gpu-runtime:cuda11.8-ubuntu20.04

Ownership and Change Process
- Any change to terraform-modules must: have a PR, pass terratest, and be approved by the module owner.
- Production infra changes require a rollout plan with canary region and rollback instructions.
- All runs that change node pools must include a preflight check script that validates quota and IAM permissions.

- CI pipeline repo: git@github.com:redwood/ci-pipelines.git (workflows/terraform).

Notes
